blocks.text: A prepaid meter in a Lagos flat ticks down in naira as the air-conditioner, the fridge and the pressing iron all draw from the same 220 V PHCN line. When the units run out you fire the generator — and you can feel, from the fuel it burns, that the iron and the kettle are the expensive loads. Power is the rate at which those appliances convert electrical energy; the disc on the old analogue meter, or the naira on the new one, is counting that energy.

blocks.markdown:
**Electrical power** $P$ is the rate of conversion of electrical energy:

$$P = \frac{W}{t} = IV$$

Using Ohm's law $V = IR$ this is written in two other forms that are worth memorising as a set:

$$P = IV = I^{2}R = \frac{V^{2}}{R}$$

- Use $P = IV$ when you know current and p.d.;
- use $P = I^{2}R$ when you know current and resistance (this is also the heating power in a wire);
- use $P = V^{2}/R$ when you know p.d. and resistance.

The SI unit of power is the **watt** (W): one watt is one joule per second. Appliance ratings are often given in watts or kilowatts ($1\ \text{kW} = 1000\ \text{W}$) together with the mains voltage, 220 V or 240 V in Nigeria.

blocks.title: The kilowatt-hour
blocks.text: The joule is too small for household bills, so electrical energy is sold in kilowatt-hours. One kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour. 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours.

blocks.caption: Electrical energy in joules, and the conversion to the commercial unit
Convert W to kW (divide by 1000) and seconds to hours (divide by 3600) before using kWh.

blocks.title: Energy in joules and the cost of a PHCN bill
blocks.prompt: A 1.5 kW electric kettle is used for 40 minutes each day. (a) Calculate the energy converted in 40 minutes, in joules. (b) If the kettle is used daily for 30 days and electricity costs ₦80 per kWh, calculate the cost of using the kettle for that month.

steps.text: (a) Convert 1.5 kW to watts and 40 minutes to seconds, then use W = Pt.
(b) Working in commercial units is quicker for the bill. Energy per day in kWh:
Energy for 30 days, then multiply by the tariff.

blocks.markdown:
### Choosing the right power formula

A lamp marked **60 W, 240 V** dissipates 60 W only when it is connected to 240 V. Its resistance is $R = V^{2}/P = 240^{2}/60 = 960\ \Omega$, and the current it then draws is $I = P/V = 60/240 = 0.25\ \text{A}$.

If the same lamp is run from a 120 V generator, the power is **not** 60 W. Resistance stays about 960 Ω, so $P = V^{2}/R = 120^{2}/960 = 15\ \text{W}$ — the lamp is dim. That is why $P = V^{2}/R$ is the right formula when the supply voltage changes but R does not.

Heating in cables and in a cell's internal resistance is $I^{2}R$. A larger current wastes much more energy as heat, which is why a short-circuit is dangerous and why transmission lines use high voltage and low current.

items: To convert joules to kWh, divide by 3.6 × 10⁶. To convert kWh to joules, multiply by 3.6 × 10⁶.
Cost in naira = (power in kW) × (time in hours) × (tariff in ₦/kWh).
A 2 kW heater running for 30 minutes uses 1 kWh, the same energy as a 100 W bulb running for 10 hours.
The rating printed on an appliance is the power it draws at its stated voltage, not at every voltage.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Keep energy in joules when the question asks for J; switch to kWh only for bills. Mixing minutes with kilowatts without converting to hours is the classic error — 1.5 kW for 40 minutes is 1.0 kWh, not 60 kWh. And P = I²R is the heating in a resistor; do not use it for an appliance unless you know both I and R.

points: Electrical power: P = IV = I²R = V²/R, measured in watts. 1 kW = 1000 W.
Electrical energy: W = Pt = IVt, measured in joules. The commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour.
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours.
Cost of electricity = energy in kWh × tariff in ₦/kWh.
An appliance's wattage is the power at its rated voltage; if the supply voltage changes, recalculate P from V²/R.
